tier_reason: The README table (Criterion, benches/benchmark.rs plus src/lib.rs) shows walkdir 68.393 ms and parallel ignore 24.728 ms against system GNU find 90.621 ms on a stated CPU with Cargo profile flags in Cargo.toml, but the rustc version and the GNU find version and build flags are not stated and the find row is not like-for-like (process spawn plus captured output), so it falls short of A; a one-star personal shootout is not a well-known independent suite, so C.

corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon E5-1630 v3 (4 cores, 8 threads with Hyper-Threading; the README calls it 8-core and says '8 physical cores'), 4-drive SATA RAID-10, ext4, warm page cache
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Cargo [profile.bench] (used by cargo bench): opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, strip symbols, debug-assertions and overflow-checks off (panic abort is set only in [profile.release], not in the bench profile); no target-cpu setting; rustc version not stated; Criterion 0.8.2; crates walkdir 2.5.0, ignore 0.4.26, jwalk 0.8.1, swdir 0.11.3, fts 0.3.0; GNU find is the distro binary, version and build flags not stated.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Serial: walkdir 68.393 ms (best estimate) vs system find 90.621 ms, about 1.3x faster (derived from page data); walkdir_minimal 69.769 ms, ignore (serial unsorted) 73.457 ms, jwalk (serial) 77.011 ms, fts_walkdir 81.623 ms. Against the in-process C fts(3) walker through the fts crate (no process spawn, no printing, the closer like-for-like C row), walkdir is about 1.19x faster (derived from page data). Parallel winner: ignore (n threads, unsorted) 24.728 ms vs find 90.621 ms, about 3.7x faster (derived from page data); swdir 25.228 ms, jwalk 26.349 ms; the README says the three parallel leaders are each roughly 2.7x faster than the quickest serial walker.
corrections.caveats: The lead calls these Go walkers; they are Rust crates (the repo benchmarks Rust walking crates and benchmarks system find as the only non-crate baseline). The find baseline is not like-for-like: src/lib.rs runs it as Command::new('find').arg(root).output(), so the find row includes process spawn and capturing every printed path through a pipe into memory, while the crate rows only iterate entries (for _ in WalkDir::new(root) {}) without printing; the README itself says find 'additionally pays process-spawn and output-formatting overhead'. That asymmetry alone could account for the 1.3x serial gap, so the serial win over find is weak; the fairer C comparison on the page is the fts_walkdir row (glibc fts(3) through FFI, no_metadata), which walkdir beats by about 1.19x. The 3.7x parallel win is threads against a single-threaded find: ignore_parallel uses num_cpus::get() threads, which is 8 logical threads on this 4-core, 8-thread Xeon E5-1630 v3 (the README's '8-core' and '8 physical cores' are wrong). GNU find version, build flags and glibc are unstated, and the rustc version is unstated. Single machine and one tree (shallow Linux kernel clone including .git); results table last updated in the 2026-06-06 commits. The bench author also wrote minifind, a parallel Rust find clone. I report ignore as the headline winner against find; walkdir is the best serial walker. The ignore entry overlaps with ripgrep's existing record (ignore is the crates/ignore member of BurntSushi/ripgrep).

notes: Numbers match the README table exactly. Shortcomings: find row charged with process spawn and output capture while crate rows print nothing; parallel win is 8 threads against single-threaded find; README misstates the CPU as 8-core (it is 4 cores, 8 threads); rustc and find versions unstated. ignore is part of ripgrep, which is already listed; consider whether the orchestrator wants this shootout as its own entry or as a second claim.
